input:
Scope
This review brings together 50 papers from the last 9 years that deal, in one way or another, with adsorbents for gas drying. In broad terms, the subject is the removal of water vapour from a gas stream by adsorption, and the focus throughout is on the adsorbent properties that determine whether a given material can dry a gas effectively and, just as importantly, whether it can continue to do so after it has been regenerated. The papers are considered against a shared set of questions. What water uptake is reported, and at what water partial pressure and temperature was it obtained? How is the adsorbent regenerated? What level of performance is reported once regeneration has taken place? And which of the quantities in a paper are measured directly, as opposed to being inferred from a breakthrough curve or from some form of model fitting? The scope is deliberately limited to adsorbent performance for drying. It does not attempt to cover full process design, vessel sizing, or economics in any systematic way, except where those topics are used by a paper to explain an adsorbent result. Materials are therefore discussed as adsorbents rather than as items in a catalogue. A material enters the discussion through its reported uptake, its regeneration behaviour, its stability, and the conditions under which those properties were measured. This framing is important because gas drying is often decided at the dry end of the bed. A large uptake under humid conditions does not, on its own, establish the property that is needed when the gas is already dry, and a good first cycle does not, on its own, establish what will happen after repeated regeneration.

Established results
Despite differences in emphasis, the established results are broadly consistent about the structure of the problem. An adsorbent intended for gas drying has to take up water strongly at low water partial pressure, it has to release that water under regeneration conditions that a real process can plausibly supply, and it has to retain a useful level of uptake after the regeneration step has been repeated. For that reason, equilibrium uptake at low partial pressure emerges as a central property, because the last section of a drying bed is working against gas that has already been substantially dried. At the same time, mass transfer cannot be separated from capacity. A material may possess adequate equilibrium capacity and still perform poorly in an actual bed if water moves too slowly into the adsorbent during loading, or if regeneration leaves part of the bed in a state that is not fully usable in the next cycle. The literature therefore tends to treat capacity, kinetics, and regeneration as connected aspects of performance rather than as wholly independent scores. Another established point is that reported uptake is always tied to conditions. Water uptake depends on partial pressure and temperature, but it can also depend on the state of the adsorbent before the measurement begins. Activation, earlier regeneration, and sample history can all shift the value that is recorded. Comparisons between papers are consequently reliable only where the measurement basis is sufficiently similar to support them. Breakthrough results require similar caution. A breakthrough curve is a result for a bed, not a pure property of a material, because it combines equilibrium behaviour, kinetics, flow distribution, bed geometry, and the threshold chosen to define breakthrough. The review accordingly treats breakthrough evidence as evidence about an adsorbent in a specified bed, not as a direct replacement for an isotherm. Finally, regeneration is not treated as a mere after-step. Heating, purge, pressure change, and time under regeneration conditions all influence how much of the initial uptake is available in the following cycle, so a drying material has to be judged by repeatable uptake as well as by the uptake it displays when fresh.

Disagreements
The disagreements in the literature are focused on one particular quantity: reports conflict on equilibrium water uptake at low partial pressure. It is important to be clear about the nature of this disagreement. The papers do not, for the most part, disagree that low-pressure uptake is important for deep drying. What they disagree about is the value that should be assigned to that uptake for comparable materials, and therefore about the ordering that results when numbers from different papers are placed next to one another. Several recurring sources of disagreement can be identified. Some papers report uptake on a dry adsorbent basis, whereas others do not state the basis with the same degree of care. Some measurements are made after a severe regeneration step and others after a milder one, so the starting state of the adsorbent is not the same before the isotherm is measured. Equilibration time is not always reported in a form that allows the reader to judge whether the low-pressure points represent true equilibrium values or only slow approaches towards equilibrium. Data reduction introduces further variation, because a value read directly from an isotherm, a value obtained from a model fit, and a value inferred from a breakthrough experiment are not strictly interchangeable, even when similar language is used to describe them. Temperature control at low partial pressure adds another layer of difficulty, since small errors in the water content of the feed gas can become large relative errors at the dry end of the measurement. For these reasons, the review does not attempt to average the conflicting values into a single representative figure. Doing so would tend to conceal the reasons for the dispute and could create a misleading impression that the quantity had been settled. The disagreement is therefore presented as a problem of measurement basis that attaches to a clearly named quantity: equilibrium water uptake at low partial pressure is reported inconsistently across the literature, and any ranking that is built on those reports inherits that inconsistency.

Gaps
The most significant gap identified by the review is the measurement that nobody reports: retained uptake after extended regeneration cycling. Many papers report an initial uptake value, and many also report uptake after one regeneration or after only a small number of cycles. What is missing is a measurement of the uptake that remains after extended cycling under clearly stated regeneration conditions, reported on the same basis as the initial uptake. In the absence of that measurement, the literature is much better equipped to compare fresh materials than to compare materials in working use. That limitation matters because a gas-drying adsorbent is, in practice, used by cycling it repeatedly. If a review cannot say how much uptake is retained after extended regeneration cycling, then the durability aspect of adsorbent selection cannot be settled from the published record alone. Several related gaps follow from the same general reporting pattern. Regeneration conditions are frequently described only loosely, cycle histories are often incomplete, and the low-pressure portion of an isotherm is sometimes represented mainly by a fitted curve rather than by measured points. These omissions also feed back into the disagreements discussed above, because where the starting state and cycle history of a sample are not reported, a dispute about uptake cannot be attributed to the material alone with any confidence. Overall, the published record is strongest where it deals with the equilibrium behaviour of fresh adsorbents and weakest where it deals with repeated use over time. The review therefore ends not with a definitive ranking, but with a reporting requirement for future work: papers should report low-pressure uptake together with its measurement basis, and should also report retained uptake after extended regeneration cycling together with the regeneration conditions, so that capacity and durability can eventually be compared on a common evidentiary footing.
